description: A self-built project by the founder of east London architecture practice TOMA Studio, this mid-terraced Victorian house has been completely re-imagined over the course of three years. The house balances refined detailing with experimentation to create a spacious and comfortable family home, which also accommodates an architecture practice and pottery studio within a Shou Sugi Ban garden room.
facilities: Handrails on one side of stairs

factsheet.heading: Self-Build Motivation
paragraphs: As an architect, I had always wanted to build my own home. After ten years of designing houses, extensions and renovations for clients across London, we wanted to take on a project that would allow us to explore the full potential of a standard, modest Victorian terrace.

The build became a full-time manual endeavour for almost three years, having originally been intended as an eighteen-month project. The ambition was to create a high-quality home for our family, but also a meaningful launch project for my own architecture practice, TOMA Studio.

The original house had not been substantially touched for almost fifty years. It was tired, dark, cellular and thermally inefficient, with an awkward plan, unusably small bedrooms and a poor connection to the garden.

Re-imagining the house from first principles led to a comprehensive rebuild. Only the front wall and a small section of the rear wall remain from the original structure. Almost everything else has been rebuilt, reconfigured or optimised, including the replacement of all floors, relocation of the staircase, adjustment of floor levels, new internal walls, resized window openings, a new dormer, rear extension, side extension and first-floor extension.

factsheet.heading: Design Approach
paragraphs: Before the project began, we lived in the house for eighteen months. This gave us time to understand the building properly: how light moved through it during the day, how it related to the garden, where there were moments of quality, and where it clearly fell short.

The original house was dark, cellular and thermally inefficient, with small rooms, awkward levels and a poor connection to the outside. Rather than treating it as a simple refurbishment, the design grew out of this period of living in the building and asking what it needed in order to fulfil its potential. The aim was to create a long-term family home and workspace.

The result is a comprehensive reworking of the house. The plan, section, structure, fabric and openings were all reconsidered, but always in response to the existing building. The ambition was to unlock the potential of a modest Victorian terrace while respecting its scale, character and mid-terrace condition.

A key part of the design was upgrading the existing fabric. The original ground floor was removed and replaced with a fully insulated slab incorporating underfloor heating. The retained external walls were subtly insulated internally. Together, these interventions have transformed the environmental performance of the house while preserving the character of the Victorian host building.

Light, ventilation and orientation were central to the design. Window openings have been enlarged and carefully positioned to bring daylight deep into the plan, while opening rooflights at the top of the house support natural stack ventilation. In the kitchen and side extension, opening windows on multiple sides, together with a small courtyard garden, create views, daylight and cross-ventilation through the centre of the house.

The project also explores a contrast between old and new. The retained parts of the Victorian house have a more familiar domestic character, refined through contemporary detailing. The new areas are more materially ambitious, using self-finished surfaces including handmade Danish buff brick, lime mortar, oak panelling, polished concrete floors and stainless-steel worktops.

travel_info: Additional travel info: The nearest Tube station is Forest Gate, on the Elizabeth Line. It has a lift at the station and is a 10 minute walk to the house.
